cite: S.F. Campaign and Governmental Conduct Code (C&GCC) §1.126(b)-(c), as amended by Ord. 129-18 (operative Jan. 1, 2019); SFEC Regulations 1.126-1 to 1.126-9
text: Current rule (since Jan. 1, 2019): a City Contractor is a person who contracts with, or seeks a contract with, any City department, SFUSD, the Community College District, or a state agency on whose board an appointee of a City elective officer sits, where the contract(s) are worth $100,000 or more in a fiscal year. Neither the contractor nor its affiliates (board members; chair, CEO, CFO and COO; anyone owning more than 10%; subcontractors listed in the bid or contract) may contribute to a City elective officer who must approve the contract (or whose board, or whose appointee's state-agency board, approves it), to a candidate for that office, or to a committee either controls. The ban runs from the submission of a proposal until negotiations end or 12 months after the contract is approved (§1.126(c)). The officer may not accept such a contribution (§1.126(d)), and a committee that does must pay it to the City (§1.126(e)). Before 2019 the rule was narrower: it covered contracts of $50,000 or more, owners of more than 20% (plus the same officers, board members, listed subcontractors and committees the party sponsored or controlled), and ran from the commencement of negotiations until negotiations ended or six months after approval. The elected officer (or board clerk) files Form SFEC-126(f)4 within five business days of approval (§1.126(f)(4)).

short: Behested payments: solicitation ban and disclosure
cite: C&GCC Art. III, Ch. 6: §3.610 (definitions) and §3.620 (solicitation ban), added by Ord. 232-21 (effective Jan. 24, 2022), re-adopted by Proposition E (June 7, 2022; effective July 10, 2022) and amended by Ord. 204-22 (effective Nov. 6, 2022); SFEC Regulations 3.620-1 to 3.620-23; Cal. Gov. Code §82015 (FPPC Form 803); Mayoral Executive Directive 20-02 (Sept. 24, 2020)
text: Solicitation ban (since Jan. 24, 2022): City elected officials, department heads, commissioners and designated employees may not directly or indirectly solicit a behested payment ($1,000 or more, or $1,000 in 12 months) from an interested party: a party, participant or agent in a permit, license or enforcement proceeding before their department (while pending and for 12 months after the decision); a City contractor of their department, or, for supervisors, a contractor whose contract the Board approves (from the proposal until 12 months after the contract term ends, capped at five years without amendment); a person who tried to influence them on a City contract (12 months); a lobbyist registered to lobby their department or a client whose lobbyist contacted it in the last 12 months; or a permit consultant who contacted it in the last 12 months (§3.620(a)). Exceptions: public appeals, competitively procured donation programs authorized by ordinance, and solicitations tied to a City contract's terms; the Board of Supervisors may grant prospective waivers of up to six months, but not for itself (§3.620(c)-(f)). Disclosure: state law requires elected officers to report on FPPC Form 803, within 30 days, payments made at their behest once one source gives $5,000 or more in a calendar year. San Francisco's own reporting (Form SFEC-3610(b), payments of $1,000 or more from interested parties) applied to commissioners from Jan. 1, 2018 (Ord. 1-17), to City elective officers as well from Jan. 1, 2019 (Ord. 129-18), and to department heads from Sept. 24, 2020 (Executive Directive 20-02); Ord. 232-21 repealed that reporting section effective Jan. 24, 2022, when the solicitation ban took its place.

short: Lobbyist registration, disclosure and contribution ban
cite: C&GCC Art. II, Ch. 1 (Lobbyist Ordinance): §2.110 (registration and monthly disclosure); §2.115(d)-(e) (contribution and bundling ban), added by Proposition T (Nov. 8, 2016), operative Jan. 1, 2018, re-enacted by Proposition D (Mar. 5, 2024), operative Oct. 12, 2024
text: Contact and expenditure lobbyists register with the Ethics Commission and file monthly reports of contacts with City officers (official, client, subject, file number, outcome sought), payments received and campaign contributions of $100 or more. Since Jan. 1, 2018, no lobbyist may make a contribution to, or deliver or transmit another person's contribution to, a City elective officer, a candidate for City elective office, or their controlled committees if the lobbyist is registered to lobby that officer's agency (or the agency the candidate seeks to join), or was so registered in the previous 90 days; a lobbyist who has not disclosed the agencies they lobby may not contribute to any City elective officer or candidate (§2.115(d)-(e)). The ban was added by Proposition T (2016) and became operative on Jan. 1, 2018; before that, lobbyists' contributions were reported but this ban did not apply.

short: Contribution limits and bans for City candidates
cite: C&GCC §1.114(a)-(b); §1.127(b) (land-use matters; Proposition F, Nov. 5, 2019, effective Dec. 20, 2019); Cal. Gov. Code §84308
text: No person other than the candidate may give more than $500 per election to a candidate committee for City office (C&GCC §1.114(a)). Corporations, LLCs and LLPs may not contribute to candidate committees (§1.114(b)). Since Dec. 20, 2019, people and affiliated entities with a financial interest of $5 million or more in a land-use matter pending before specified boards may not contribute to members of the Board of Supervisors, the Mayor, the City Attorney, candidates for those offices, or their controlled committees, from the start of the matter until 12 months after the final decision (§1.127(b)). State law (Gov. Code §84308) limits contributions from parties and participants in license, permit and contract proceedings to officials who decide them. Ballot-measure and independent-expenditure committees not controlled by a candidate are not subject to the $500 candidate limit.
